title: Did you choose your career or just the next job?
author: Luca Foppoli
summary: Luca Foppoli, in his Worth Arguing With series, asks corporate professionals whether they ever actually chose their career or merely drifted from one next step to the next. He opens with a high performer who made VP in her late twenties and quit at 33 when her body and conscience forced the decision, and with a friend fifteen years into increasingly senior roles who still feels short of his potential. His argument is that even people who deliberately choose at every step, as he did, are choosing inside a frame they never questioned. He draws on Erich Fromm's idea of modern man freed from old authorities but not freed to chart his own path, so that we take the path of least resistance and adopt the desires it proposes, such as the promotion and the bigger title. Noticing the frame is hard, like not perceiving motion on a smooth train, until something hits you. He ends by urging readers to listen to the stubborn inner voice that says there could be more, and to remake the choice daily rather than age passively.
points: Choosing deliberately at each career step is not the same as choosing the frame itself, and both the drifter and the planner can end up inside a frame neither examined.
Fromm's point that we are free from old authorities but not free to chart our own path explains why people adopt the desires the career path proposes, such as promotions and bigger titles.
Frames are invisible for the same reason a smooth train feels motionless, so the signal to question one usually arrives as a shock like burnout, a bad boss or a body that fails.
Choosing is not a single event but something that must be remade every day, and the first step is listening to the quiet voice that says this is not the whole thing.
quotes: Eventually we all choose, even if it is mostly because we are forced to - think of a bad boss or a better offer.
Yet, even when we do choose, we keep choosing within the same frame.
You drifted while I chose, yet we both ended up in the same place: inside a frame neither of us ever questioned.

In 1941 the German psychoanalyst Erich Fromm described the condition of modern man as freed from the old authorities, from the Church to traditional morality, but not freed to chart a path on his own.
Do you perceive being in motion when standing on a train? No, unless the train rocks a little. Same here: oblivion, until something hits you.
If you listen closely, you will hear a feeble, stubborn voice telling you that this doesn’t need to be the whole thing, that there could be more, that you could be more.
Whether it begins is in your hands. Whether it continues is a choice you have to remake every day.
